query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, reactive Ti/Ni coating to the tungsten surfaces in a W–Cu composite will enable the in situ formation of a graded intermetallic interface during consolidation that suppresses phase separation and interfacial void formation, thus enhancing thermal conductivity under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten–copper composite with discrete tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix.
generation.intervention: Depositing a tailored thin Ti/Ni (or Ni-based) intermetallic-forming coating on the tungsten particles or ligaments prior to consolidation (e.g., by magnetron sputtering).
generation.conditions: The composite is processed by consolidation methods such as spark plasma sintering and then operated under service conditions characterized by high-temperature heat transfer and irradiation, as encountered in joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components.
generation.structural_mediator: A graded interfacial region formed by controlled interdiffusion and reaction between the coating, tungsten, and copper, leading to a stable intermetallic layer that minimizes microstructural defects.
generation.mechanism: The Ti/Ni coating promotes interfacial diffusion and chemical reactions during consolidation, leading to the formation of a graded intermetallic layer. This layer reduces interfacial stress, inhibits the formation of detrimental voids, and prevents phase separation between tungsten and copper. As a result, the effective thermal conductivity is improved compared to untreated composites.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated composite should exhibit a lower incidence of phase separation and interfacial voids, maintaining or even increasing thermal conductivity relative to an untreated composite when subjected to high-temperature cycling and irradiation.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites that, under similar processing and operating conditions, show significant phase separation and interfacial void formation leading to reduced thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable within the processing limits of typical consolidation techniques (such as spark plasma sintering) and service conditions relevant to plasma-facing and cooling joints. Its performance may be limited if the coating thickness or composition is not optimally controlled, or if excessive diffusion degrades the designed graded interface over extended irradiation exposure.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness, deposition parameters, and detailed reaction kinetics during consolidation remain to be fully determined, which may affect the robustness of interface formation and the magnitude of thermal conductivity improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one set with tungsten surfaces pre-coated with the Ti/Ni layer and one set without any coating. Process both sets under identical consolidation conditions (e.g., via spark plasma sintering). Subject the specimens to cyclic high-temperature and irradiation testing that simulates the conditions in plasma-facing joints.
measurements: High-resolution microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to quantify phase separation and interfacial void formation
Thermal conductivity measurements under simulated service conditions
Irradiation damage assessment via appropriate spectroscopy or imaging techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti/Ni-coated composites do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in phase separation/interfacial voids or fail to exhibit improved thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite across the testing conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn this study, an effective way of applying Ti/Ni deposited coating to the surface of diamond single crystal particles by magnetron sputtering was proposed and novel high-entropy alloy (HEA)/diamond composites were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The results show that the interfacial bonding state of the coated diamond composite is obviously better than that of the uncoated diamond composite. Corresponding mechanical properties such as hardness, density, transverse fracture strength and friction properties of the coated diamond composite were also found to be better than those of the uncoated diamond composite. The effects of interface structure and defects on the mechanical properties of HEA/diamond composites were investigated. The research directions for further improving the structure and properties of high-entropy alloy/diamond composites were proposed. Keywords: high-entropy alloy, diamond, coating, interface, mechanical properties

Diamond single crystal particles with Ti/Ni coatings were obtained by magnetron sputtering. The diamond gained more than 30% weight and the coating thickness was 10–20 μm. The interfacial diffusion and solid solution formation in coated diamond composites led to the increase of interfacial bonding strength. The interface bonding strength and mechanical properties of the composites without diamond coating decreased, due to the occurrence of graphitization at the interface and the formation of carbides. Compared with the composite with uncoated diamond, the density, hardness, transverse fracture strength and interfacial bonding properties of the composite with coated diamond were significantly improved. The wear resistance of the coated composites is obviously higher than that of the uncoated composites, because the coating on the diamond particles maintains a relatively complete crystal form in the SPS process and has a higher bonding strength with the HEA matrix. This improves the holding force of the matrix and gives full play to the excellent properties of the HEA.

decision.trend: Several composite systems have suffered from weak interfacial bonding that leads to phase‐separated or voided junctions, degrading macroscopic properties. Early work in diamond/HEA composites (PMC7514646) showed that applying a thin, reactive metallic coating (Ti/Ni) on the reinforcement not only improved the interfacial diffusion but led to stronger chemical bonding and a better load transfer. In contrast, untreated composites or those requiring multi‐step procedures have struggled to meet the performance demands under combined thermal cycling and irradiation. Although multiphase or multi‐stage approaches have been attempted in related systems, they have proven impractical under the processing and service constraints of joint applications.
decision.unsolved: A single, robust method that can prevent phase separation and interfacial void formation in tungsten–copper composites remains elusive. Specifically, a treatment that yields a graded interface resistant to the harsh thermal and irradiation conditions, without requiring post‐processing or multiple sequential interventions, is still needed.
decision.lever: apply a tailored, thin intermetallic-forming coating (for example, a Ni-based or Ti/Ni composite layer) onto the tungsten particles or ligaments prior to consolidation
decision.why: Given the encouraging results in analogous systems (as in PMC7514646), this single intervention is likely to promote an in situ formation of a graded tungsten–copper interface during processing. Such a graded interlayer would mitigate deleterious phase separation and void formation while enhancing interfacial bonding and thermal conductivity under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
